open-question.question: The "Codex manifest location" decision places the manifest template at scripts/hosts/codex/.codex-plugin/plugin.json rendered to the same relative path, while the "Codex install route" decision puts the plugin under plugins/cairn/ so the manifest lands at plugins/cairn/.codex-plugin/plugin.json, and templates render to their own relative path. Where does the Codex manifest template sit, and where in the committed hosts/codex/ tree does the manifest land?
open-question.recommendation: The build already renders every template to its own relative path, so a template under plugins/cairn/ lands the manifest beside the skills with no build change, and the definition directory reads as a copy of the published repository, whose README and marketplace templates already sit at tree-root paths. Only the literal template path in the "Codex manifest location" decision is corrected; the manifest still sits at .codex-plugin/plugin.json relative to the plugin root.
open-question.alternative: The Codex manifest template sits at scripts/hosts/codex/plugins/cairn/.codex-plugin/plugin.json and, like every other template, renders to that same relative path, so the manifest lands at hosts/codex/plugins/cairn/.codex-plugin/plugin.json. The build stays unchanged. The "Codex manifest location" decision is read as placing the manifest at .codex-plugin/plugin.json relative to the plugin root, and only its template path is corrected. The tree still has no plugin.json at its root or at the plugin root. No build change is needed. The existing rule that a template renders to its own relative path already puts the manifest beside the skills/, agents/, shared/ and tools/ directories that the [layout] places under plugins/cairn/. The definition directory then reads as a copy of the published repository, with the repository-root marketplace and README templates at its top and the plugin manifest under plugins/cairn/. The plugins/cairn prefix is written twice, once in the [layout] values of settings.toml and once in the template's directory path, and both must be kept in step by hand. No build check catches a manifest that ends up away from the skills it describes. The literal template path recorded in the "Codex manifest location" decision is also superseded.

The Codex manifest template stays at scripts/hosts/codex/.codex-plugin/plugin.json, as the "Codex manifest location" decision records. The build changes so that renames entries can move rendered templates as well as rendered core/ files: today renames run before templates are added, and a template source fails with "which the layout does not produce". The Codex settings.toml then carries one renames entry that moves .codex-plugin/plugin.json to plugins/cairn/.codex-plugin/plugin.json, so the manifest lands at hosts/codex/plugins/cairn/.codex-plugin/plugin.json. The Claude Code and Antigravity renames lists stay empty, so their trees render byte-identically. Both recorded decisions keep their literal wording: the template sits where "Codex manifest location" puts it, and the manifest lands where "Codex install route" puts it. The build gains no new settings key, because it widens an existing per-file mechanism. It is a build change that the "Codex manifest location" decision explicitly said was not needed. It broadens what renames means, and the docstring and settings comments that describe renames as moving layout output must be updated. The template's location in the definition directory also no longer shows where it lands, so a reader has to cross-reference settings.toml to find out.

The build gains a new settings key, declared by every host because the key set is strict, that names the plugin's subdirectory inside the host tree. It is plugins/cairn for Codex and empty for Claude Code and Antigravity. Templates are split into two groups: those under a dedicated part of the definition directory render below that subdirectory, and the rest render to their own path from the tree root. The Codex manifest template sits in the plugin-side group at .codex-plugin/plugin.json and lands at hosts/codex/plugins/cairn/.codex-plugin/plugin.json. The two existing hosts render byte-identically because their subdirectory is empty. Where the plugin sits inside a host tree is declared once, in one key, instead of being implied by the layout values and template paths. The manifest template keeps the plugin-relative path .codex-plugin/plugin.json, and a later host with a marketplace-wrapped layout reuses the mechanism without hand-mirrored paths. This is the largest build change of the set. It adds a key to all three settings.toml files, adds a template-grouping rule to the build and its docstring, and contradicts the "no build change" reasoning in the "Codex manifest location" decision. How much of it pays off depends on whether the build otherwise learns a plugin-subdirectory concept, which is the axis the "Plugin-root check offset" question owns.

open-question.question: The "Verification run mode" decision has the maintainer run "the one inline skill" by hand in an interactive Codex session, approving its git steps, but no decision names which skill; the README example, init-milestone-base-workflow, would do nothing useful in a verification workspace already seeded with a milestone. Which cairn skill does the interactive verification check run?
open-question.recommendation: It takes no argument, like the README's example invocation, so the $cairn: form is checked in the shape a user types. It runs several open-question tool subcommands under the sandbox and ends in an approved commit, which backs both sandbox claims, and on a one-question seed it makes a single commit because the sort leaves a one-block document as it is. Its input is the real output of the alternatives dispatch, the seed stays as the "Verification workspace" decision describes it, and the question is left standing.
open-question.alternative: The interactive check runs `$cairn:recommend-all-open-questions`. The maintainer runs it after the headless alternatives dispatch has embedded alternatives into the seed's one bare question. The skill picks one option inline, writes it with the open-question tool's `embed`, `lift` and `sort` subcommands, and commits under `Recommendation-annotation:`, plus a `Question-ordering:` commit if the sort moved a block. The seed itself is unchanged. It covers the most Codex paths in one run. Several `python3 ${PLUGIN_ROOT}/tools/open_questions.py` subcommands run under the sandbox, which backs the claim that the tools need only read access to the plugin directory. Inline reading of `${PLUGIN_ROOT}/shared/recommend-procedure.md` works with no agent involved. The run also produces at least one approved commit. It is the step that naturally follows the alternatives dispatch, so its input is the real output of an earlier check rather than something staged for the test. It can only run after the alternatives dispatch has succeeded, so a failed or quota-stopped dispatch also blocks the inline check. Whether that order fits depends on how the maintainer's step is placed relative to the task list, which a sibling question owns. Its inline reasoning over the whole set and its possible second commit make it one of the heavier runs on a free-tier quota, and it brings in more approval prompts than a single-commit skill.

The interactive check runs `$cairn:answer-open-question-with-alternative`. The maintainer runs it on the seed's question after the headless alternatives dispatch has embedded its alternatives, naming one of the embedded alternative ids. The skill calls the tool's `lift --alternative`, folds the decision into `## Decisions` through the answer procedure, removes the block with `remove --option`, and makes one `Alternative-answer:` commit. The seed is unchanged. It is a single-commit, inline run that still calls the open-question tool through `${PLUGIN_ROOT}` (both `lift` and `remove`) and reads a shared procedure. That backs both sandbox claims and the `$cairn:` invocation form with one approval round and little model work. Its input is the alternatives dispatch's real output, and the maintainer types only an id that is already on the page. It also depends on the alternatives dispatch having succeeded first, which ties it to an order that the sibling question on placement relative to the task list must allow. It removes the seed's only question, so any later re-run of the alternatives dispatch (for example after a fix) needs the workspace seeded again. Because the maintainer chooses the alternative, it exercises a skill-only path that no headless line in the docs uses.

The interactive check runs `$cairn:answer-open-question` with a Short Title and an answer the maintainer types. It runs on the seed's question after the headless alternatives dispatch. The skill records the literal answer through the answer procedure, gives its own verdict on whether the answer settles on one of the embedded alternatives, removes the block with the tool, and makes one `Manual-answer:` commit. The seed is unchanged. It exercises the most commonly used recording skill and the shared answer core through `${PLUGIN_ROOT}`. A tool call runs under the sandbox and there is one approved commit. The answer is free text, so the check does not depend on what the alternatives dispatch happened to produce. It could even run on the bare question if the order demanded it. If it runs before the alternatives dispatch, it consumes the seed's only bare question and leaves that dispatch with nothing to do. So in practice it still has to follow the dispatch, which is an order the sibling question on task-list placement must allow. The maintainer also has to compose an answer to a throwaway question, and the result depends on how the model judges that answer rather than on a fixed lift.

The interactive check runs `$cairn:review-milestone-requirements` on the seeded milestone after both headless dispatches. The skill reasons over `requirements.md` and the question document, lists blocks and may add or remove them through the tool, and commits under `Requirements-review:` if it changed anything. The seed is unchanged. It is the workflow's central loop skill and calls the open-question tool more than any other inline skill, so it is a broad test of tool calls under the sandbox and of `${PLUGIN_ROOT}` resolution in an interactive session. What it does depends on the model's judgment. On a tiny seed it may decide the milestone has converged and change nothing, which leaves no git step to approve, and the check then fails to back the git-approval claim that the run mode relies on. Questions it adds would stay bare unless the alternatives dispatch ran again, which costs quota. It reasons over the whole milestone, so it also uses more of the free-tier quota than a recording skill.

The interactive check runs `$cairn:init-milestone-base-workflow`, the README's example invocation. To make that run meaningful, the no-model seed creates `milestones/`, the milestone directory and its question and task, but no `milestones/README.md` and no `AGENTS.md`. The maintainer runs the bootstrap first. It checks git and `python3 --version`, creates `milestones/README.md` with the pointer set to `none`, creates `AGENTS.md` with the Milestone Workflow section, and commits under `Workflow-bootstrap: milestones`. The runner then sets the pointer to the seeded milestone by a no-model edit before the headless dispatches. It is the first command the Codex README tells users to type, so the documented invocation is checked on the exact text a new user meets. It is also the only skill that writes the Codex-only `AGENTS.md` wording, so it checks the context-file slot live. It can run first, with no dependency on either headless dispatch succeeding. It runs no open-question tool and executes nothing from the plugin's `tools/` directory, so it does not back the sandbox claim that `python3` tools need only read access to the plugin. It also requires changing the seed the Verification workspace decision describes, and adding a hand-edited pointer step between the inline check and the dispatches that the verification itself introduces.

The interactive check runs `$cairn:submit-task` with a one-line issue. The maintainer runs it after the headless `complete-all-tasks` dispatch has completed the seed's one task. The skill writes one brief-level section into `TASKS_TODO.md` from the shared task format and makes one commit. The seed is unchanged. It is a cheap, single-commit inline run that is fully predictable. It needs no question in any particular state, and it reads a shared procedure through `${PLUGIN_ROOT}` and asks for exactly one git approval. It calls no Python tool, so it does not back the sandbox claim about the plugin's tools. If it ran before the `complete-all-tasks` dispatch, that run would complete two tasks and use more than the one dispatch per agent the four-check budget allows, which forces an order the sibling question on task-list placement must allow. It also leaves a task open in a workspace that is deleted afterwards.

No skill is named now. The verification task's brief keeps "one inline skill", and the completion runner or the maintainer picks the skill when the verification runs, based on the workspace's state at that point. It commits to nothing before the headless dispatches have shown what state they leave behind. If one of them fails, the inline check can be switched to a skill that does not depend on the failed check, with no decision to reopen. Which inline skill runs determines whether the seed needs changing and how the inline check must be ordered against the dispatches, and leaving it open defers both. The runner deriving the task has no recorded criterion, so the check may end up on a skill that backs neither sandbox claim. This direction amounts to postponing the choice, not removing it.

open-question.question: The live verification mixes runner-executed checks (the plugin install and two headless agent dispatches) with one check the maintainer must run by hand in an interactive session, and a headless complete-all-tasks run has no one to pause for. open-question.recommendation: The whole verification is derived into the initial batch, so the maintainer's check is listed in TASKS_TODO.md and no clean end-of-run report can hide it. The three runner outcomes are committed at a task boundary before the pause, so the dispatches never run twice and a quota stop resumes from committed state. The brief of the interactive-check task says it passes only when the workspace shows that the maintainer ran the inline skill interactively, such as the commit that skill leaves in the workspace's git history. The runner can ask the maintainer directly and follow up on an unclear result in conversation instead of guessing from leftover files. The complete-task procedure has no step for waiting on a person, so the pause depends on the inline runner choosing to ask. The same task run through complete-all-tasks would have no one to ask. The verification is missing from the derived batch, so its existence again depends on the maintainer remembering to submit it. A long single task that waits on a person also has no committed checkpoint if the quota runs out partway.

This rejects the premise of a headless run. The whole task list, including a final verification task that holds all four checks, is completed by the maintainer with complete-task, one task at a time, in an interactive cairn session. complete-all-tasks is not used for this milestone. When the verification task reaches the interactive check, the runner pauses for the maintainer, takes the outcome from the conversation and the workspace, and records all four in one entry. Every task, the verification included, is derived into the initial batch and run by someone who can be asked. No task fails by design and none is added later. It gives up unattended completion for the whole milestone just to handle one step. The maintainer has to drive every task of a long batch by hand. Nothing in the list stops a later complete-all-tasks call from reaching the verification task headless, where it has no one to ask.
